Context/Background:
We leverage a clinical trial that compared neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 (Nivo), anti-PD-1+CTLA-4 (Nivo+Ipi), and anti-PD-1+LAG-3 (Nivo+Rela) therapies in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma patients. Combination therapies promote higher pathologic response rates versus monotherapy, and major pathologic response is associated with better survival. To address whether successful immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) regimens act through similar or distinct pathways, we robustly and longitudinally characterize transcriptional and proteomic dynamics of CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in a clonal manner. 

Thirty-eight patients were evaluable for pathologic tumor response (pTR) and categorized into three groups following previous studies: pTR-0 (91–100% viable residual tumor), pTR-1 (51%–90% viable residual tumor), and pTR-2 (≤50% viable residual tumor. 

To study the association between transcriptional dynamics of T cells and pathologic responses to neoadjuvant ICI treatments, we isolated and profiled 372,914 CD45+CD3+ TIL from 35 patients (29 baseline and 31 post-surgical fresh tumor specimens; 20 patients having matched pre- and post-treatment biopsies), using the 10x Genomics 5′ scRNA-seq workflow. These cells were clustered into five distinct populations annotated as CD8+ T, CD4+ T, FOXP3+ T, γδ T/MAIT and cycling T cell clusters, and visualized by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) analysis. Clusters were annotated based on the expression of reported canonical T cell marker gene and CITE-seq expression levels.
Prompt:
We analyzed the clusters of CD3+ TIL and found that the proportion of baseline CD8+ TIL showed a trend to the more frequent in responding patients.  When we assessed baseline expression of PDCD1, CTLA4, and LAG3 by CD8+ TIL, we observed the highest expression for PDCD1 and LAG3. The expression of PDCD1 and LAG3 by baseline CD8+ TIL positively correlated with the degree of pathologic response only in Nivo+Rela-treated patients. Similar analyses did not show a significant correlation between LAG3, PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression levels in baseline CD8+ TIL and the degree of pathologic response in the Nivo and Nivo+Ipi cohorts.

To identify baseline CD8+ TIL transcriptional signatures correlating with pathologic response, we generated a list of differentially expressed genes (DEG) between pTR-2 and pTR-0 tumors for each regimen.

Based on the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between pTR-2 and pTR-0 tumors for the Nivo+Ipi and Nivo+Rela cohorts, generate a summary describing the key transcriptional signatures, functional categories, and immune pathways enriched in pTR-2 vs pTR-0 tumors. Highlight representative genes and link them to their biological roles.  Focus on T cell–specific functional programs and gene modules defined by known immune states.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
We compared baseline CD8⁺ TIL transcriptional profiles between patients achieving major pathologic response (pTR-2, ≤50% viable tumor) versus non-responders (pTR-0, >90% viable) in two neoadjuvant ICI regimens: Nivolumab+Ipilimumab (Nivo+Ipi) and Nivolumab+Relatlimab (anti–PD-1+anti–LAG-3, Nivo+Rela). All samples derive from treatment-naïve head and neck squamous cell carcinoma tumors; scRNA-seq libraries generated with the 10× Genomics 5′ workflow. Definitive cohort sizes and exact patient numbers are not specified in the DEG files.  

Keywords  
• Interferon response  
• Chemokine signaling  
• Effector cytotoxicity  
• Protein synthesis/proliferation  
• T cell exhaustion  

Candidate Genes  
PDCD1, LAG3, CXCL13, MX1, GZMB  

Summary of Key Transcriptional Signatures  

1. Nivo+Ipi (anti–PD-1 + anti–CTLA-4) cohort—pTR-2 vs pTR-0:  
   ­– Enrichment of ribosomal and translational initiation programs (e.g., RPS26, RPL13A), reflecting heightened protein synthesis in proliferating T cells.  
   ­– Upregulated mitochondrial ribosomal genes (MTRNR2L8), consistent with metabolic remodeling supporting T cell expansion.  
   ­– Modest elevation of broad “immune activation” GO terms, but comparatively weaker induction of chemokine/IFN-driven pathways.  

2. Nivo+Rela (anti–PD-1 + anti–LAG-3) cohort—pTR-2 vs pTR-0:  
   ­– Strong type I/II interferon‐stimulated gene signatures (e.g., MX1, IFIT1/3), signaling robust antiviral‐like activation within TIL.  
   ­– Prominent chemokine and tissue‐organizing module upregulation (CXCL13, CCL4), hinting at tertiary lymphoid structure formation and B/T cell cross‐talk.  
   ­– Potent induction of cytotoxic effector genes (GZMB, PRF1) and co‐inhibitory receptors (PDCD1, LAG3)—a hallmark of effector/exhausted T cell states.  
   ­– Enriched antigen processing and presentation pathways (HLA class I/II, TAP1), supporting enhanced tumor antigen recognition.  

Functional Categories & Immune Pathways  
– “Ribosome”/“Translation” (hallmark MSigDB): selectively up in Nivo+Ipi pTR-2, linking CTLA-4 blockade with proliferative T cell expansion.  
– “Interferon Gamma Response” and “IFN-α Response” (MSigDB Hallmark): uniquely enriched in Nivo+Rela pTR-2, anchoring a Th1-polarized antiviral program.  
– “Chemokine‐mediated Signaling” (GO BP) and “Cytokine–Cytokine Receptor Interaction” (KEGG): dominant in Nivo+Rela pTR-2, underpinning T cell recruitment and lymphoid niche formation.  
– “Cytotoxic T cell–mediated Killing” (Reactome): Nivo+Rela-specific, reflecting upregulation of perforin/granzyme‐driven pathways.  

Representative Gene Roles  
– MX1: archetypal ISG driving antiviral state and antigen‐presenting cell recruitment.  
– CXCL13: chemoattractant for B cells and T follicular helper cells; fosters tertiary lymphoid structures.  
– GZMB/PRF1: mediators of granule-dependent target cell lysis—definitive effector function.  
– RPS26, MTRNR2L8: markers of active translation and metabolic reprogramming in proliferating T cells.  
– PDCD1, LAG3: co-inhibitory checkpoints marking a terminally differentiated/exhausted phenotype.  

Across both regimens, pTR-2 tumors share a core T cell activation axis, but diverge in the balance between proliferative versus effector/exhausted states: Nivo+Ipi skews toward a biosynthetic–proliferative program, whereas Nivo+Rela unleashes a robust interferon-driven cytotoxic and chemokine network.  

Implications  
These data suggest that LAG-3 co-blockade may prime CD8⁺ TIL for enhanced tumor cytotoxicity and tertiary lymphoid structure formation, while CTLA-4 co-blockade predominantly augments T cell proliferation. Such mechanistic divergence could guide rational combination strategies—e.g., pairing proliferation‐focused regimens with agents that sustain effector differentiation or tissue organization.  

Next Steps & Clarifications  
1. Validate by flow cytometry whether proliferative markers (Ki-67) versus effector molecules (granzyme B) differentially mark CD8⁺ TIL in pTR-2 tumors across regimens.  
2. Assess tertiary lymphoid structure prevalence by spatial transcriptomics or multiplex immunofluorescence in Nivo+Rela responders.  
3. Examine whether the proliferative signature in Nivo+Ipi persists post-treatment or transitions into an exhausted state.  
4. Clarify involvement of memory T cell modules (e.g., IL7R, TCF7) not captured in baseline DEGs.
